p: Editions differ over whether to add "disciples." The meaning is the same.

why: The manuscripts are divided, and the editors weigh them differently. This translation follows the SBL text it is based on. Tischendorf noted that Matthew elsewhere prefers "the twelve disciples" (10:1; 11:1; 20:17), while Mark 14:17 has "the Twelve," which may have influenced copyists. Nothing turns on the choice.

p: Older manuscripts say Jesus "blessed" the bread; the Byzantine text says he "gave thanks."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Textus Receptus (KJV "blessed it"); Codex Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Bezae, Regius (L), Z, the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions (reported by Tischendorf)
Byzantine majority; Codex Alexandrinus, E, F, H, K, M, S, U, V, Δ and more than 130 later manuscripts (reported by Tischendorf)

why: "Blessed" has the older witnesses and matches Mark 14:22. "Gave thanks" matches Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24 and the next verse, and the church's word "Eucharist," so a copyist would easily write it.

t: The covenant or the new covenant?
p: The KJV says "the new testament." The oldest manuscripts do not have "new" in Matthew.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), according to Metzger; Vaticanus, Regius (L), Z, 33 and 102 (reported by Tischendorf)

readings.en: my blood, that of the new covenant
readings.plain: my blood, the blood of the new covenant

why: "New" was probably added from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25, which have "the new covenant." If it had been original, there would be no reason to drop it. The shorter form echoes Exodus 24:8 directly.
b: The KJV's "testament" translates diathēkē, which can mean a will or a covenant. Here it means covenant, as in Exodus 24:8.

p: Later manuscripts and the KJV give the governor's full name.

why: Matthew names him only "Pilate" everywhere else. The full name, familiar from the creeds and from Luke 3:1 and Acts 4:27, was easily added at his first mention. Tischendorf himself thought the full name original; most modern editors do not.

p: Some old manuscripts and translations have Judas say "righteous blood."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "innocent blood"); Codex Alexandrinus, the first hand of Vaticanus, Ephraemi and most manuscripts, the Syriac and Gothic, Eusebius and Chrysostom (reported by Tischendorf)

A corrector's note in the margin of Codex Vaticanus, Regius (L), the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic and Armenian, Origen, Cyprian and Lucifer (reported by Tischendorf); also Codex Koridethi (Θ), according to Metzger

why: "Innocent blood" is the phrase of the Greek Old Testament (Deuteronomy 27:25; Jeremiah 19:4) and fits Pilate's "I am clean" (athōos, 27:24). "Righteous" probably came from 23:35 and 27:19. As Tischendorf asked, who would have written "innocent" if "righteous" stood in the text?

t: Into the sanctuary or in the temple?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say Judas threw the silver down "in the temple."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Codex Vaticanus, Regius (L) and a few others, Origen and Eusebius (reported by Tischendorf)
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "in the temple"); Codex Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and most later manuscripts, the Latin versions (reported by Tischendorf)

why: "Into" is the harder reading: it has Judas hurl the coins into the holy place itself, where he could not go. "In" softens it. The note on 27:5 discusses what naos means here.

t: Jeremiah, Zechariah, Isaiah, or no name?
p: Almost all manuscripts say "Jeremiah," though the words are mostly from Zechariah. A few change or drop the name.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Bezae and nearly all Greek manuscripts, most Old Latin, the Vulgate, Coptic and Gothic, Eusebius (reported by Tischendorf); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus
Codex Beratinus (Φ, 500s), according to Metzger; 33, 157, Old Latin a and b, some Syriac copies, and copies Augustine knew (reported by Tischendorf)
Minuscule 22 and the margin of the Harclean Syriac (reported by Tischendorf and Metzger)
Minuscule 21 and Old Latin l (reported by Metzger and Tischendorf)

why: "Jeremiah" has overwhelming support, and it is the harder reading: copyists who knew the words were from Zechariah had a reason to change it, and none to introduce it. Augustine already knew copies without the name and judged that the name belonged. See the note on this verse for why Matthew may have named Jeremiah.

p: Some manuscripts, and copies Origen knew, call him "Jesus Barabbas." Most manuscripts say only "Barabbas."

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 (NA28 in brackets); minuscules 1, 118, 209, 241 and 299, the Palestinian Syriac and Armenian, known to Origen (reported by Tischendorf); Codex Koridethi (Θ, 800s) and the Sinaitic Syriac, according to Metzger
Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV); Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae and most manuscripts, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic and Peshitta (reported by Tischendorf)

why: The longer reading is followed, as in the SBL and NA28, because it is hard to explain as an addition: no scribe would give a criminal the name Jesus, while many would remove it out of reverence. Origen says exactly that the name should not be given to a sinner. The Tyndale House edition, weighing the much larger and older support for "Barabbas," prints the short form, as Tischendorf did.
b: This goes with 27:17, where the same manuscripts read "Jesus Barabbas" a second time. In 27:17 Codex Vaticanus has "the Barabbas" (ton Barabban), and the article looks like the remains of "Jesus the Barabbas," which supports the longer reading.

p: Goes with 27:16: the same manuscripts call him "Jesus Barabbas" here too.

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 (NA28 in brackets); minuscules 1, 118, 209, 241 and 299, the Palestinian Syriac and Armenian, Origen in Latin (reported by Tischendorf); Codex Koridethi (Θ), according to Metzger
Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV); most manuscripts; Codex Vaticanus reads "the Barabbas" (reported by Tischendorf)

why: See 27:16. Pilate's question is sharper with two men called Jesus, which fits Matthew's taste for parallels: "Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus, the one they call the Messiah?"

p: Many manuscripts have Pilate call Jesus "this righteous man," echoing his wife's words in 27:19.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28; Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, 102, Old Latin a and b, Chrysostom (reported by Tischendorf); Codex Koridethi (Θ) and the Sinaitic Syriac, according to Metzger

readings.en: of the blood of this righteous one

why: The shorter reading is followed, with the SBL and NA28, because "righteous" looks like an addition drawn from 27:19. The manuscripts that have it put it in different places, which suggests it was added. The Tyndale House edition prints the longer reading, and the case is close.

p: The KJV says "vinegar mingled with gall." The oldest manuscripts say "wine."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae and others, according to Metzger
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "vinegar"); Codex Alexandrinus and most later manuscripts, according to Metzger

why: "Sour wine" brings the verse closer to Psalm 69:21 ("they made me drink vinegar") and to 27:48. Copyists were more likely to make that change than the reverse. Mark 15:23 has "wine."

a: shared out his clothes by throwing lots.
t: The prophecy added in the KJV
p: The KJV quotes Psalm 22:18 here. The words are not in the oldest manuscripts or in most Byzantine ones.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority; Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and most manuscripts, according to Metzger

readings.en: casting lots, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots
readings.plain: shared out his clothes by throwing lots. This happened so that what was spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled: "They divided my clothes among them, and over my clothing they threw lots."

why: The quotation was copied in from John 19:24, which has nearly the same words, and given Matthew's usual formula. The oldest and the great majority of manuscripts lack it; even the Byzantine text does not have it. Erasmus's printed Greek, the basis of the KJV, included it.

p: The Byzantine majority text adds the Pharisees to the mockers at the cross. The KJV does not.

why: The older text's bare statement is biting sarcasm. "If" was probably added from 27:40 ("If you are God's Son") to make the sense plainer.

p: Most manuscripts give the Hebrew "Eli." Codex Vaticanus and a few others have Mark's Aramaic "Eloi." The spelling of "lema" also varies.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28; "Eli" in Codex Alexandrinus and most manuscripts, "lema" in Codex Vaticanus, Regius (L) and 33 (reported by Tischendorf)
Westcott-Hort; Codex Vaticanus, 33, a few others and the Coptic (reported by Tischendorf), as in Mark 15:34

Byzantine majority and Tischendorf ("lima"); Codex Alexandrinus, K, U, Δ and most later manuscripts. The Textus Receptus has "lama" with Bezae and some Old Latin copies (KJV "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani") (reported by Tischendorf)
Codex Bezae, with the Old Latin "zapthani" (reported by Tischendorf)

why: "Eli" has wide and early support and is the harder reading in a Gospel that copyists knew alongside Mark's "Eloi." It also explains the bystanders' mistake (27:47): "Eli" sounds like "Elijah." Vaticanus' "Eloi" is best explained as harmonizing with Mark. "Lema," "lima" and "lama" are spellings of the same Aramaic or Hebrew word for "why"; Bezae's "zaphthani" reflects the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1 (azavtani).

p: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus add that a soldier pierced Jesus' side before he died. Most manuscripts lack it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV); Codex Alexandrinus, Bezae and most later manuscripts, most Latin and Syriac copies (reported by Tischendorf)

Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), Ephraemi (400s), Regius (L, 700s), Γ, 1010 and a few others, according to Metzger; also U, minuscules 5, 48, 67, 115 and 127, some Vulgate manuscripts, the Palestinian Syriac and the Ethiopic; known to Chrysostom (reported by Tischendorf); printed in double brackets by Westcott and Hort
readings.orig: σώσων αὐτόν. ἄλλος δὲ λαβὼν λόγχην ἔνυξεν αὐτοῦ τὴν πλευράν, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὕδωρ καὶ αἷμα
readings.en: to save him. And another took a spear and pierced his side, and water and blood came out
readings.plain: is coming to save him." Another man took a spear and stabbed his side, and water and blood came out.

why: Although two of the oldest manuscripts have it, almost all editors judge it an early addition from John 19:34, perhaps first written in a margin. In John the spear comes after Jesus' death; here it would come before, and seem to cause it, which conflicts with 27:50. The wide support for the shorter text in other early witnesses decides it.
b: This is one of the rare places where modern editions reject a reading found in both Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Tischendorf reports that Severus of Antioch, in the 500s, told of a debate over these words in Constantinople that was settled by consulting an old copy of Matthew which lacked them.

p: The KJV and Byzantine text call her son Joses, as in Mark 15:40. The SBL and NA28 have Joseph.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28; the first hand of Codex Bezae, Regius (L), 157 and a few others, the Old Latin, Vulgate, Coptic and Ethiopic, the margin of the Harclean Syriac (reported by Tischendorf)
Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Joses"), Tischendorf; Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and most manuscripts (reported by Tischendorf)
A corrector of Codex Bezae (reported by Tischendorf), as in Mark 15:40

why: Joses is a short form of Joseph, so it is the same name either way. Copyists may have changed Joseph to Joses to match Mark 15:40, or the reverse to match 13:55. Tischendorf suggested a reason for the second: some early readers, among them John Chrysostom, took this Mary to be Jesus' own mother, and writing "Joseph" made her sons match the brothers named in 13:55. The SBL and NA28 judge Joseph original here.

a: had been made a disciple of Jesus
t: "Was made a disciple" or "was a disciple"?
p: The SBL and NA28 say Joseph "had been made a disciple"; the Byzantine text and the KJV say he "was Jesus' disciple."

why: This translation follows the SBL text. The passive matches the verb Jesus uses for making disciples in 28:19, while the active, intransitive use ("to be a disciple") is older Greek. Tischendorf noted that both forms are found. The meaning differs only slightly: the passive hints that someone made Joseph a disciple.

Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "where the Lord lay"); Codex Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae, Regius (L) and most later manuscripts, the Latin and Syriac versions (reported by Tischendorf)
